lead.headline: A Faraway Star Explodes
lead.deck: Telescopes spotted a new supernova in a galaxy 50 million light-years away.
body: Stars are giant balls of glowing gas. Some end their lives in a huge explosion called a supernova. On November 2, astronomers spotted a brand new one.

So where did this explosion happen? It is in a galaxy called NGC 1433. A galaxy is a giant family of stars. It is a spiral, about 50 million light-years from Earth. A light-year is how far light travels in one year, so that is very far.

How did people find it? A set of robotic telescopes called ATLAS first reported it. Then astronomers used the Keck telescope to work out what kind of supernova it was. It is called a Type Ia supernova.
Scientists learned the star had not yet reached its brightest point. On November 9, Gemini South, a telescope in Chile, took a picture of the galaxy and the supernova.

map.caption: A telescope in Chile imaged the galaxy and its new supernova.

lead.why: Catching a supernova early lets scientists study how these big explosions begin.

world.headline: A Warm Ocean Patch Grows Strong
world.deck: The WMO says El Niño is heading for record strength.
body: El Niño is a pattern of warm water in the tropical Pacific Ocean. It changes rain and heat in many places.

Now a weather group is giving a warning. The World Meteorological Organization, called the WMO, studies weather and climate. It says El Niño has grown stronger since August and expects record strength by December.
The WMO says extreme weather is more likely into 2027. It says El Niño is almost certain to last until February 2027.
El Niño can bring floods to some places and dry spells to others. A France 24 news report from November 25 told of droughts in the Pacific and flooding in San Francisco.
The WMO also shows how warm our world already is. The past four years, 2023 to 2026, are the four warmest on record. Sea levels are the highest since satellites began measuring in 1993.

us.headline: The US Loses a Measles Title
us.deck: Measles now spreads steadily in the United States, a health group says.
body: Measles is a sickness that spreads very easily from person to person. A vaccine protects against it. On November 17, the Pan American Health Organization said measles now spreads steadily in the United States, Mexico and Bolivia.
So all three lost their "elimination status," a title for countries that have stopped measles spreading steadily. A country loses it when the same virus passes between people for 12 months or more.
The United States has reported more than 5,400 measles cases, and 10 people have died. About 92 in every 100 US kindergartners had the vaccine in 2025. In 2019, it was 95.
About 95 in 100 are needed to block the spread. The CDC says the risk is highest where fewer people have the shot. The US can win its title back by stopping the spread for 12 months.

science_and_technology.headline: An Old Probe Is One Light-Day Away
science_and_technology.deck: Voyager 1 is so far from Earth that light takes a whole day to reach it.
body: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe, a machine sent to explore space. On November 18, it reached one light-day from Earth. That is the distance light travels in one day.
How far is that? Voyager 1 was about 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion kilometres) from Earth. That is so far that a message from Earth takes a whole day to reach it.
But the old probe has a problem. It makes its power with a special generator, and the power is slowly fading. Each Voyager probe loses about 4 watts of power every year.
So engineers keep switching off parts to save power. In April 2026, they shut down an instrument called LECP. The cameras were turned off back in 1990. Two science instruments still worked in April.
science_and_technology.why: By switching off parts, engineers help an old probe keep sending news from very far away.
